capacitor-discharge-time.formula: V(t) = V0 e^(-t/RC); t_discharge = R C ln(V0/V_safe); R_max = t_limit / (C ln(V0/V_safe)); P_continuous = V0^2/R. V0 is the voltage at disconnect, the peak (1.414 x rms) on an ac bank.
capacitor-discharge-time.edition: The capacitor stored-energy discharge requirement of NEC 2023 460.6 and 460.28 -- residual voltage to 50 V within 1 minute at 1,000 V nominal or less, 5 minutes above 1,000 V, by a permanent or automatic discharge means -- by name. A computational aid; the AHJ-adopted NEC edition and the equipment listing govern.
capacitor-discharge-time.freeAccess: NEC is free to read at nfpa.org/freeaccess. The RC-discharge relation is first-principles; the 460.6 time limits and the permanent/automatic-connection requirement are in the published code.
capacitor-discharge-time.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
capacitor-discharge-time.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Time limit
assumptions.value: residual to 50 V within 1 minute at 1,000 V nominal or less, 5 minutes above 1,000 V (600 V was the pre-2020 threshold)

assumptions.name: Connection
assumptions.value: the discharge means must be permanently connected or connect automatically on loss of line; a manually switched bleed does not comply

assumptions.name: Continuous power
assumptions.value: the resistor dissipates V0^2/R while the bank is energized (about half that on an ac bank with a peak V0); rate it with margin

assumptions.name: Initial voltage
assumptions.value: an ac bank can be disconnected at its peak, sqrt(2) x rms; the rms value returns a resistor too large

feed-conversion-ratio.formula: total_gain = final_weight - initial_weight; ADG = total_gain / days_on_feed; FCR = total_feed / total_gain (lb feed per lb gain).
feed-conversion-ratio.edition: Standard livestock production metrics (average daily gain, feed conversion ratio) per USDA / land-grant extension animal-science references, by name.
feed-conversion-ratio.freeAccess: ADG and FCR are standard extension-published production formulas.
feed-conversion-ratio.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
feed-conversion-ratio.editionNote: Two performance metrics over a feeding period: average daily gain ADG = (final - initial weight) / days on feed (lb/day), and feed conversion ratio FCR = total feed fed / total weight gained (lb of feed per lb of gain, so a lower FCR is more efficient). Feed is entered on the basis the operation tracks: as-fed (bunk weight) is standard; multiply as-fed by the ration dry-matter fraction for a dry-matter-basis FCR. FCR is not constant - it rises as an animal finishes because fat gain costs more feed per pound than lean growth - so a whole-period FCR blends the growth curve, and the breed, ration energy, and environment (cold, heat, health) drive the real numbers. A benchmarking aid, not a ration formulation.

assumptions.name: ADG
assumptions.value: (final - initial weight) / days on feed

assumptions.name: FCR
assumptions.value: total feed / total gain, lb feed per lb gain; lower is more efficient

assumptions.name: Feed basis
assumptions.value: as-fed is standard; convert to dry matter with the ration DM fraction

fuel-tax-ifta.formula: Taxable gallons = jurisdiction miles / fleet MPG; net tax = taxable gallons x rate - gallons purchased x rate (a negative net is a credit).
fuel-tax-ifta.edition: IFTA Articles of Agreement quarterly-return method, by name.
fuel-tax-ifta.freeAccess: Free at iftach.org; the base jurisdiction's return governs.
fuel-tax-ifta.governance: Math aid for personal verification. The ELD on the truck and the carrier tariff are the legal record. State limits may be lower than federal.
fuel-tax-ifta.editionNote: Single-edition (the per-jurisdiction taxable-gallon method; rates change quarterly and are user-supplied - run per jurisdiction and sum the net column).

assumptions.name: Tax rate
assumptions.value: per-jurisdiction $/gal, user-supplied (rates change quarterly)

insulation-heat-loss.formula: R_cond = ln(r2/r1) / (2π × k); h_outside = h_conv + h_rad; R_outside = 1 / (h_outside × 2π × r2); Q = (T_s − T_a) / (R_cond + R_outside). Since 2026-10-09 h_outside is the bare-pipe-heat-loss model: Churchill-Chu natural convection for a horizontal cylinder with air properties at the film temperature, Churchill-Bernstein forced convection for the air velocity, combined as the cube-root sum of cubes, and h_rad = eps × σ × (T_s⁴ − T_a⁴)/(T_s − T_a). Iterate for the outer-surface temperature.
insulation-heat-loss.edition: ASHRAE Handbook Fundamentals chapter 25 (insulation) by name; ASTM C680 (cylindrical surface conditions) by name; manufacturer k-values from data/hvac/insulation-k-values.json.
insulation-heat-loss.freeAccess: ASTM C680 licensed; manufacturer technical bulletins free at each manufacturer site.
insulation-heat-loss.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.
insulation-heat-loss.editionNote: Single-edition (engineering practice + manufacturer k-values; quarterly recheck of manufacturer attribution).

assumptions.name: Stefan-Boltzmann constant σ
assumptions.value: 0.1714×10⁻⁸ BTU/(hr·ft²·°R⁴)

assumptions.name: Default jacket emissivity
assumptions.value: 0.9 (painted steel / fabric jacket)

assumptions.name: Film air properties
assumptions.value: Sutherland viscosity and conductivity at the film temperature, 1 atm (the bare-pipe-heat-loss model); until 2026-10-09 a simplified ASHRAE form with standard-air properties, which read 5 to 17% higher in convection on small pipe

assumptions.name: Iterative outer-surface T solve
assumptions.value: 12 fixed-point iterations for the R_outside ↔ T_s2 coupling

sanitary-dfu.formula: total DFU = sum(fixture count × DFU value). Minimum pipe size = smallest size whose table maximum ≥ total DFU: horizontal branch and stack per IPC Table 710.1(2); building drain per IPC Table 710.1(1) (slope-dependent).
sanitary-dfu.edition: IPC 2021 (International Plumbing Code). Section 710; DFU values per IPC Table 709.1; capacities per Tables 710.1(1) and 710.1(2).
sanitary-dfu.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
sanitary-dfu.editionNote: Bundled DFU and capacity tables follow IPC 2021. Jurisdictions on UPC or an older IPC edition differ at the margins; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: DFU values
assumptions.value: IPC Table 709.1 (private WC 3, public WC 4, lavatory 1, bath 2, shower 2, kitchen sink 2, urinal 4, floor drain 2, ...)

assumptions.name: Branch / stack capacity
assumptions.value: IPC Table 710.1(2) max DFU by nominal size

assumptions.name: Building-drain capacity
assumptions.value: IPC Table 710.1(1) max DFU by size and slope (1/8 / 1/4 / 1/2 in per ft)

window-overhang-shade.formula: tan(profile) = tan(altitude) / cos(surface-solar azimuth); shade_line = projection x tan(profile); shaded = clamp(shade_line - gap, 0, glass_height); sunlit_fraction = 1 - shaded/glass_height. No direct beam when altitude <= 0 or |surface-solar azimuth| >= 90.
window-overhang-shade.edition: The ASHRAE Handbook-Fundamentals (Fenestration) and ACCA Manual J profile-angle / shade-line method for overhang shading of vertical glazing, by name.
window-overhang-shade.freeAccess: The profile-angle relation is first-principles solar geometry; it is computed here from the entered sun position rather than read from a proprietary shade-line-factor table.
window-overhang-shade.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
window-overhang-shade.editionNote: Overhang shading of vertical glazing by the profile-angle (shade-line) method. With the wall outward normal as x, the sun direction is (cos a cos g, cos a sin g, sin a) for altitude a and surface-solar azimuth g; projecting that onto the vertical plane normal to the wall gives the profile angle, tan(profile) = tan(a)/cos(g). The overhang casts its shade line projection x tan(profile) below its underside, and the part of that falling past the gap onto the glass is shaded. At normal incidence (g = 0) the profile angle equals the solar altitude. The shade-line factors ASHRAE tabulates by latitude and orientation are NOT used - the angle is computed directly from the entered sun position, which sidesteps the table. SCOPE: this returns the DIRECT-BEAM sunlit fraction. Shaded glazing still receives diffuse sky and ground-reflected radiation, so multiplying a TOTAL solar gain by this fraction overstates the reduction; apply it to the beam component and retain the diffuse term. Assumes an overhang wide enough that end effects are negligible, no side fins, no adjacent obstructions, and flat vertical glazing. A design aid, not a Manual J or a full fenestration analysis.

assumptions.name: Profile angle
assumptions.value: tan(profile) = tan(altitude)/cos(surface-solar azimuth); equals the altitude at normal incidence

assumptions.name: Shade line
assumptions.value: projection x tan(profile) below the overhang; the portion past the gap shades the glass
assumptions.source: ASHRAE / ACCA Manual J shade-line method

assumptions.name: Beam only
assumptions.value: the reported fraction is direct-beam; diffuse sky and ground-reflected radiation still reach shaded glass

assumptions.name: Geometry limits
assumptions.value: overhang wide enough to ignore end effects; no side fins or adjacent obstructions

standpipe-friction.formula: Total = elevation (0.434 psi/ft × height) + friction in one outlet's hose line (NFA CQ²L). Lines on separate outlets run in parallel, so their friction does not add; the riser carries their combined flow, n × Q. Riser-pipe friction and the valve/appliance loss are not included. Min residual at the topmost outlet 100 psi for Class I per NFPA 14 §7.8 (Minimum and Maximum Pressure Limits; §7.10 is flow rates).
standpipe-friction.edition: NFPA 14 (2024) §7.8 (Minimum and Maximum Pressure Limits) and §7.10 (Flow Rates) by name and section.
standpipe-friction.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.
standpipe-friction.editionNote: Editions available: NFPA 14-2024 is the current published edition; earlier editions (2019 / 2016 / 2013) carry slightly different residual-pressure requirements; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Class I min residual
assumptions.value: 100 psi at the topmost outlet

reach-range.formula: forward unobstructed: 15 to 48 in. Forward obstructed: 48 in maximum where the reach depth is 20 in or less, 44 in where it exceeds 20 in, and the reach depth may not exceed 25 in. Side unobstructed: 15 to 48 in. Side obstructed: 48 in maximum to a reach depth of 10 in, 46 in from there to a reach depth of 24 in, with the obstruction itself 34 in high maximum and 24 in deep maximum.
reach-range.edition: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, 308 Reach Ranges (308.2.1, 308.2.2, 308.3.1, 308.3.2). A US federal standard in the public domain, quoted directly.
reach-range.freeAccess: The 2010 ADA Standards are published in full at no cost at ada.gov and by the US Access Board.
reach-range.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
reach-range.editionNote: Where an outlet, switch, thermostat, dispenser, or control may sit is four rules rather than one number, and which one applies turns on the direction of approach and on what is in the way. Two of the four behave in ways people do not expect. On a forward reach, past 25 in of reach depth there is NO permitted height at all - the element does not need to come down, it needs to move, and lowering it accomplishes nothing because no height complies. On a side reach the obstruction has its own ceiling, and that is the number that ends arguments: it may be no more than 34 in high and 24 in deep, so a standard 36 in counter is too TALL to be reached over under this section whatever the height of the thing behind it. The section allows exactly two exceptions to that height: the top of washing machines and clothes dryers may be 36 in maximum, and operable parts of fuel dispensers may be 54 in maximum measured from the surface of the vehicular way where the dispensers are installed on existing curbs. The band edges are steps rather than slopes - 20 in of forward depth permits 48 in and 20.1 in permits only 44 - so trimming a couple of inches of depth can buy four inches of height, which the tile reports. The low limit catches the other end and is the one missed on rough-in: 15 in minimum above the finish floor, so a receptacle set at the framer's habitual 12 in fails. Every one of these ranges presumes a clear floor or ground space of the right size and orientation is actually there - a forward reach needs a forward approach and a side reach needs a parallel one - and without it the range does not apply at all. Not checked: that clear floor space; the 5 lbf operating force and the requirement that operable parts work with one hand and without tight grasping, pinching, or twisting of the wrist; which elements are operable parts and which are exempt; kitchen and kitchenette work surfaces, appliances, and storage, which are governed by their own sections; knee and toe clearance under a forward approach; and state and local accessibility law and the electrical code, which sets its own mounting heights for different reasons. A reach check, not a rough-in schedule.

assumptions.name: Forward unobstructed
assumptions.value: 48 in maximum high, 15 in minimum low

assumptions.name: Forward obstructed
assumptions.value: 48 in to a 20 in reach depth, 44 in beyond, 25 in maximum depth

assumptions.name: Side unobstructed
assumptions.value: 48 in maximum high, 15 in minimum low

assumptions.name: Side obstructed
assumptions.value: 48 in to a 10 in reach depth, 46 in to a 24 in reach depth

assumptions.name: Obstruction on a side reach
assumptions.value: 34 in high maximum and 24 in deep maximum

assumptions.name: Exceptions to the 34 in
assumptions.value: washing machine and dryer tops 36 in; fuel dispenser operable parts 54 in on existing curbs

accessible-parking-count.formula: Table 208.2 by lot total: 1-25 -> 1; 26-50 -> 2; 51-75 -> 3; 76-100 -> 4; 101-150 -> 5; 151-200 -> 6; 201-300 -> 7; 301-400 -> 8; 401-500 -> 9; 501-1,000 -> 2% of the total; 1,001 and over -> 20 plus 1 for each 100 or fraction thereof over 1,000. Van spaces = ceil(required accessible / 6) per 208.2.4. The table is applied to each parking facility separately.
accessible-parking-count.edition: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, 208.2, Table 208.2, and 208.2.4. A US federal standard in the public domain, quoted directly.
accessible-parking-count.freeAccess: The 2010 ADA Standards are published in full at no cost at ada.gov and by the US Access Board.
accessible-parking-count.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
accessible-parking-count.editionNote: Two rules run here and the second is the one that gets skipped. Table 208.2 sets the accessible count from the lot total, and 208.2.4 then requires that 'for every six or fraction of six parking spaces required by 208.2 to comply with 502, at least one shall be a van parking space complying with 502.' FRACTION OF SIX is the operative phrase: four accessible spaces still owe one van and seven owe two, and a van space is one OF the accessible spaces rather than an extra beyond them. Two branches of the table also get missed. From 501 to 1,000 spaces it stops being a lookup and becomes 2% of the total, which produces a step at the seam - the last table row (401 to 500) gives 9, while 501 spaces at 2% is 10.02 and rounds up to 11, so one space added to a 500-space lot adds two accessible spaces. Above 1,000 it is 20 plus one for each 100 or fraction thereof over 1,000. The fractional results round up throughout, because a count of spaces cannot be fractional and rounding down would provide fewer than the standard requires. The third thing people get wrong is the unit of counting: the table applies PER PARKING FACILITY, not per site. Four separate lots of 26 spaces owe eight accessible spaces where the same 104 spaces in a single lot would owe five, so splitting parking into separate lots raises the requirement rather than lowering it. Not checked: the geometry of the spaces under 502 - space and access-aisle widths, the wider space or wider aisle a van requires, the vertical clearance a van needs along its whole route in, surface slope, and signage; whether the spaces sit on the shortest accessible route to the entrance and are dispersed among entrances under 208.3; the higher ratios that apply at hospital outpatient, rehabilitation, and residential facilities under 208.2.1 through 208.2.3; and state and local requirements, several of which exceed these. A count, not a layout.

assumptions.name: Counting unit
assumptions.value: each parking facility separately, not the site total

assumptions.name: 501 to 1,000 spaces
assumptions.value: 2% of the total, rounded up

assumptions.name: Over 1,000 spaces
assumptions.value: 20 plus 1 for each 100 or fraction thereof over 1,000

assumptions.name: Van share
assumptions.value: one for every six or fraction of six accessible spaces required

assumptions.name: Van spaces
assumptions.value: counted within the required accessible spaces, not in addition to them

time-alignment.formula: Speed of sound c = 331.3 + 0.606 × T_C (m/s). Delay-tower delay (ms) = (d_main − d_delay)_m / c × 1000 + the Haas offset. Haas-window offset 10-30 ms recommended for delayed system natural-source perception.
time-alignment.edition: Classical acoustics; AES (Audio Engineering Society) information documents on time-alignment by name.
time-alignment.freeAccess: AES information documents free at aes.org/standards/blog.
time-alignment.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

assumptions.name: Default temperature
assumptions.value: 68 °F (20 °C) unless user supplies

chi-square-independence.formula: Expected E[i][j] = row_total_i * col_total_j / N; chi-square = sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected) on (r-1)(c-1) degrees of freedom; p-value = 1 - chi2Cdf(chi-square, df). Cramer's V = sqrt(chi-square / (N * min(r-1, c-1))).
chi-square-independence.edition: OpenIntro Statistics 4th ed. Chapter 6 (inference for categorical data, two-way tables) by name; the chi-square CDF via the regularized lower incomplete gamma function per Numerical Recipes in C 2nd ed. §6.2. Verified against scipy.stats.chi2_contingency (correction=False).
chi-square-independence.freeAccess: OpenIntro Statistics free at openintro.org; Numerical Recipes chapters free at numerical.recipes.
chi-square-independence.governance: Estimate only. Readability formulas and similar metrics are derived from a representative population and have known edge-case noise. The classroom teacher governs final text selection, grade placement, and assessment decisions.
chi-square-independence.editionNote: The test of independence works on an r x c contingency table (two categorical variables cross-tabulated) and asks whether the row and column variables are associated. It differs from goodness-of-fit in two ways: it builds its own expected counts from the margins (E = row total x column total / N, the counts under independence) rather than taking an expected distribution as input, and its degrees of freedom are (r-1)(c-1) rather than k-1. Cramer's V rescales chi-square to a 0-to-1 association strength. The chi-square approximation degrades when an expected cell drops below 5; the tile flags it and suggests combining categories or Fisher's exact test. This tile does not apply the Yates continuity correction, so a 2x2 result matches scipy's chi2_contingency with correction=False.

assumptions.name: Expected from margins
assumptions.value: E[i][j] = row_total_i * col_total_j / N (the counts under independence)

assumptions.name: Degrees of freedom
assumptions.value: (r-1)(c-1) for an r x c table

assumptions.name: Effect size and scope
assumptions.value: Cramer's V = sqrt(chi2/(N min(r-1,c-1))); no Yates correction (matches scipy correction=False); expected cells should be at least 5

motor-unbalance-derate.formula: v_avg = (Vab + Vbc + Vca)/3; unbalance% = max deviation from v_avg / v_avg x 100; derate_factor read off the NEMA MG-1 curve (1% -> ~0.98, 5% -> ~0.75), interpolated; over 5% -> do not operate.
motor-unbalance-derate.edition: Motor derating for voltage unbalance, NEMA MG-1; the unbalance per the NEMA definition (max deviation from the average over the average), by name.
motor-unbalance-derate.freeAccess: The NEMA MG-1 derate curve is read off the standard; above 5% unbalance the motor should not be operated. The manufacturer and MG-1 govern the final figure; correct the unbalance source first.
motor-unbalance-derate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.

assumptions.name: Unbalance definition
assumptions.value: maximum deviation of any line-to-line voltage from the three-phase average, divided by the average

assumptions.name: Derate curve
assumptions.value: the bundled MG-1 derating points (1/2/3/4/5% -> ~0.98/0.95/0.88/0.82/0.75), linearly interpolated

soil-swell-shrink.formula: loose = bank x (1 + swell/100); load_factor = 1/(1 + swell/100); compacted = bank x (1 - shrink/100); fill_shortage = bank - compacted.
soil-swell-shrink.edition: Caterpillar Performance Handbook soil-conversion method (swell / shrinkage / load factor) by name; first-principles volume conversion.
soil-swell-shrink.freeAccess: The swell / shrinkage / load-factor concept is published earthmoving practice. The percentages come from the geotech report or a published soil table.
soil-swell-shrink.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
soil-swell-shrink.editionNote: Swell and shrinkage are soil properties, not constants - wet clay, dry sand, and shot rock differ widely. The load factor converts a loose truck ticket back to bank yards for earned-quantity payment. Compaction to a spec is verified in the field, not assumed.

assumptions.name: Soil percentages
assumptions.value: swell (sand ~12, common earth ~25, clay ~30, rock ~50+) and shrinkage (~10-20) from the geotech report

battery-inverter-dc-conductor.formula: dc_current_a = inverter_power_w / (battery_voltage_v x efficiency_pct/100); min_conductor_ampacity_a = 1.25 x dc_current_a; ocpd_a = next standard size (NEC 240.6) >= 1.25 x dc_current_a.
battery-inverter-dc-conductor.edition: NEC 690.8(B) (continuous current), 706 (energy storage systems), 240.4 (conductor protection), and 240.6 (standard OCPD sizes), by name; the inverter and battery datasheets and the AHJ govern.
battery-inverter-dc-conductor.freeAccess: The DC-current relation is Ohm's/power law (public); the 125% continuous factor and the standard OCPD sizes are public NEC, and the inverter power, efficiency, and battery voltage come from the datasheets.
battery-inverter-dc-conductor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
battery-inverter-dc-conductor.editionNote: The DC conductor and overcurrent device between a battery bank and an off-grid or energy-storage-system inverter. The inverter's full-output DC input current is its AC output power divided by the battery bank voltage and the inverter efficiency -- a lower bank voltage (24 V vs 48 V) pulls proportionally MORE current for the same power. NEC 690.8(B) / 706 / 240.4 size both the conductor and the overcurrent device at 125% of that continuous current, and 240.6 rounds the OCPD up to the next standard size. A battery can deliver an enormous fault current, so the DC overcurrent device is typically a LISTED DC-rated fuse (often Class T) with an adequate interrupting rating, paired with a DC-rated disconnect. The run should be short and heavy for voltage drop and terminated at the battery manufacturer's torque. This is a sizing estimate; the inverter and battery datasheets, the available fault current and interrupting rating, the AHJ, and the adopted NEC edition govern the final design.

assumptions.name: 125% continuous
assumptions.value: conductor and OCPD at 1.25 x the DC input current; OCPD to the next standard size (240.6)

assumptions.name: DC-rated / Class T
assumptions.value: a battery's high fault current needs a listed DC-rated fuse (often Class T) and disconnect with adequate interrupting rating

rolled-blank.formula: Developed flat length L = pi x neutral-axis diameter; with the neutral axis k x T from the inside, D_neutral = OD - 2T(1-k) = ID + 2kT. Default k = 0.5 (mid-thickness) gives L = pi x (OD - T).
rolled-blank.edition: Developed blank length to roll plate into a cylinder - first-principles arc-length geometry as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; public domain.
rolled-blank.freeAccess: Pure arc-length geometry, public; the diameter, thickness, and k-factor are user-supplied.
rolled-blank.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rolled-blank.editionNote: First-principles arc-length at the neutral axis. The k-factor (default 0.5 mid-thickness) shifts the neutral axis inward for tighter rolls; edge trim and seam-weld gap are added separately.

assumptions.name: Neutral axis
assumptions.value: the neutral axis sits k x thickness from the inside face (default k = 0.5)

compound-miter.formula: Crown cut flat on the saw: miter (table swing) = atan(sin(spring) / tan(corner/2)); bevel (blade tilt) = asin(cos(spring) x cos(corner/2)). Spring is the molding profile angle (38 or 45 deg), corner is the wall angle (90 deg square).
compound-miter.edition: Compound-miter geometry for crown molding cut flat - first-principles trigonometry; public domain. Reproduces the standard published compound-miter chart.
compound-miter.freeAccess: Pure trigonometry, public; the spring angle and wall corner angle are user-supplied.
compound-miter.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
compound-miter.editionNote: First-principles trigonometry, verified against the standard compound-miter chart (38 deg spring / 90 deg corner gives 31.62 deg miter and 33.86 deg bevel; 45 / 90 gives 35.26 / 30.00). The angle magnitudes are the same for inside and outside corners; only the workpiece orientation changes. Cut a scrap test corner first.

assumptions.name: Cut flat
assumptions.value: the molding lies flat on the saw table (not sprung against the fence); the spring angle is the molding's installed angle from the wall

alternator-charging-load.formula: idle_out = alternator x idle_frac; cruise_out = alternator x cruise_frac; balance = output - total_load; idle_frac ~0.5, cruise_frac ~0.9.
alternator-charging-load.edition: Automotive/marine alternator charging-balance practice (alternator output-vs-RPM curves) by name; first-principles load balance.
alternator-charging-load.freeAccess: The output-fraction rule of thumb and the load-balance arithmetic are standard published automotive-electrical results.
alternator-charging-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
alternator-charging-load.editionNote: An alternator's output depends on rotor speed, so at engine idle it makes only a fraction of its rated output (commonly around half) and near cruise most of it (around 90%). The charging balance = available output - total continuous electrical load: a negative idle balance means the battery supplies the shortfall at idle or at a stoplight (headlights, blower, ignition, audio, accessories), and a positive cruise balance means the battery recharges while driving. If the idle balance is negative and the vehicle idles a lot or runs a big accessory load, step up the alternator or shed load. The output fractions are rules of thumb; the alternator's actual output-vs-RPM curve and the real duty cycle govern.

assumptions.name: Output fractions
assumptions.value: ~50% of rated output at idle, ~90% at cruise (rotor-speed dependent)

assumptions.name: Load balance
assumptions.value: balance = output - total continuous load; negative at idle drains the battery

assumptions.name: Curve governs
assumptions.value: the alternator's actual output-vs-RPM curve and the real duty cycle govern

hydroplaning-speed.formula: spin-down (rolling wheel) Vp = 9 sqrt(P) knots = 10.35 sqrt(P) mph; spin-up (locked wheel) onset Vp = 7.7 sqrt(P) knots; P = tire inflation pressure (psi). 1 knot = 1.1507794 mph.
hydroplaning-speed.edition: Dynamic hydroplaning speed per NASA Technical Note D-2056 (Horne & Dreher, 1963) and FAA Advisory Circular AC 91-6A, by name; both public.
hydroplaning-speed.freeAccess: NASA TN D-2056 and FAA AC 91-6A are public-domain U.S. Government documents; the relation depends only on the user's tire pressure.
hydroplaning-speed.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hydroplaning-speed.editionNote: The speed at which a tire rides up on a water film and loses contact with the road. The NASA/FAA relation depends only on tire inflation pressure: a rolling wheel loses traction near Vp = 10.35 sqrt(P) mph (9 sqrt(P) knots), the spin-down value usually quoted as the hydroplaning speed, while a stationary or locked wheel begins to hydroplane earlier near 7.7 sqrt(P) knots, so hard braking into standing water is the worse case. A truck tire at 100 psi hydroplanes near 104 mph, a car tire at 32 psi near 59 mph, and an underinflated 24 psi tire near 51 mph, which is why low pressure is dangerous in rain. This is a screening figure assuming standing water at least about 0.1 in deep and smooth or worn tread; deeper water, bald tires, or smooth pavement lower it, while good tread channels water and raises it. A safety screen; road conditions and the driver govern.

assumptions.name: Spin-down speed
assumptions.value: Vp = 9 sqrt(P) knots = 10.35 sqrt(P) mph (rolling wheel), P in psi

assumptions.name: Spin-up onset
assumptions.value: Vp = 7.7 sqrt(P) knots (locked/stationary wheel), the more conservative onset

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: assumes ~0.1 in standing water and smooth/worn tread; a screening figure, not a tread-and-water-depth model

run-capacitor-microfarad.formula: measured_uf = 1e6 x I / (2 x pi x 60 x V) ~= 2652 x measured_amps / measured_volts (the in-circuit capacitance from Xc = 1/(2 x pi x f x C) at 60 Hz). Band = rated_uf x (1 +/- tolerance%/100); within / below / above gives the good / weak / replace verdict.
run-capacitor-microfarad.edition: First-principles capacitive reactance (public); +/-6% run-capacitor tolerance is the common motor-capacitor convention (by name).
run-capacitor-microfarad.freeAccess: The capacitive-reactance relation is public physics; the tolerance is an editable field convention.
run-capacitor-microfarad.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
run-capacitor-microfarad.editionNote: Single-edition (the capacitor nameplate and the equipment manual govern; discharge before handling).

assumptions.name: Frequency
assumptions.value: 60 Hz line frequency (the 2652 constant is 1e6 / (2 x pi x 60))

assumptions.name: Tolerance
assumptions.value: default +/-6% for run capacitors (editable); start capacitors use a wider band

assumptions.name: Measurement
assumptions.value: amps by clamp on a capacitor lead and volts across its terminals with the unit running; replace with equal microfarad and equal-or-higher voltage rating

winch-drum-line-pull.formula: Dn = drum_dia + (2n - 1) x rope_dia; Pn = rated_pull x (drum_dia + rope_dia) / Dn (the rating is the first-layer figure at the first wrap's centerline); Vn = first-layer speed x Dn / (drum_dia + rope_dia); wraps_per_layer = floor(barrel_width / rope_dia).
winch-drum-line-pull.edition: Wire-rope drum mechanics / SAE winch rating convention, by name.
winch-drum-line-pull.freeAccess: Drum line-pull mechanics are a public engineering result; the winch manufacturer's layer ratings govern.
winch-drum-line-pull.governance: Estimate. Head rigger and manufacturer working-load-limit charts govern. Inspect every piece of hardware before the show.
winch-drum-line-pull.editionNote: The rated line pull is a bare-drum figure for the first wrap and it falls layer by layer as the growing moment arm works against the motor (outer layers can be 30-40% weaker) while the line speed rises in proportion; the rope must also fit the drum capacity. A planning aid, not the winch's certified capacity.

assumptions.name: Mean-diameter model
assumptions.value: Dn = drum + (2n-1) x rope_dia; pull inversely proportional to mean diameter, referenced to the first layer at drum + rope_dia

assumptions.name: Layer ratings govern
assumptions.value: the winch manufacturer's published per-layer ratings are authoritative

crane-load-radius-boom.formula: load_radius = boom_foot_offset + boom_length x cos(boom_angle); boom_tip_height = boom_foot_height + boom_length x sin(boom_angle); angle_for_target_radius = acos((target_radius - boom_foot_offset)/boom_length).
crane-load-radius-boom.edition: Crane boom geometry (load radius and tip height from boom length and angle), by name; the manufacturer's load chart and the load-moment indicator govern the rated capacity.
crane-load-radius-boom.freeAccess: The radius/height relations are public plane trigonometry; the boom length, angle (off the boom-angle indicator), and geometry offsets are the operator's measured values.
crane-load-radius-boom.governance: Estimate. Head rigger and manufacturer working-load-limit charts govern. Inspect every piece of hardware before the show.
crane-load-radius-boom.editionNote: The load radius -- the horizontal distance from the crane's center of rotation to the hook -- is what the load chart is indexed by, but the operator reads a boom ANGLE off the boom-angle indicator. This converts between them: load radius = the boom-foot horizontal offset from the center pin + boom length x cos(boom angle), and the boom-tip height = the boom-foot height + boom length x sin(boom angle). The inverse gives the boom angle that lands the hook at a target radius, acos((target radius - offset)/boom length), and flags a target beyond the boom's reach. A 30 ft boom at 60 degrees off a foot 4 ft out and 6 ft up gives a 19 ft radius and 32 ft tip height; lowering to 45 degrees swings out to 25 ft. CRITICAL LIMITATION: this is rigid-boom geometry. It does NOT account for boom deflection under load (the boom bends and the real radius grows), wire-rope stretch, tire or outrigger settling, or an out-of-level machine -- all of which INCREASE the actual operating radius beyond the geometric value, reducing capacity. The crane's load chart, the load-moment indicator, the manufacturer's deflection data, and a qualified operator and lift director govern the rated capacity at radius.

assumptions.name: Rigid-boom geometry
assumptions.value: radius = offset + L cos(angle); tip height = foot height + L sin(angle); inverse angle = acos((target - offset)/L)

assumptions.name: Deflection excluded
assumptions.value: boom deflection, rope stretch, and out-of-level all INCREASE the real radius; the load chart and load-moment indicator govern

plant-spacing-count.formula: s_ft = spacing_in / 12; square_n = ceil(bed_ft2 / s_ft^2); triangular_n = ceil(bed_ft2 / (0.866 x s_ft^2)), 0.866 = sqrt(3)/2.
plant-spacing-count.edition: First-principles square- and triangular-grid relations with nursery / landscape estimating references for the staggered-grid 0.866 factor (by name); no edition cycle.
plant-spacing-count.freeAccess: The square- and triangular-grid relations are public planting-estimating practice; the 0.866 = sqrt(3)/2 row offset is the equilateral staggered grid.
plant-spacing-count.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
plant-spacing-count.editionNote: Single-edition (the grid relations and the 0.866 factor do not roll). The spacing comes from the plant's mature spread or the planting plan, edge plants are rounded up so the bed is covered, and this is a planting-density count, not an irrigation or fertilization rate.

assumptions.name: Square grid
assumptions.value: plants = bed area / spacing^2 (rows and columns square)

assumptions.name: Triangular grid
assumptions.value: plants = bed area / (0.866 x spacing^2); the 60-degree staggered rows pack about 15% more plants

assumptions.name: Spacing
assumptions.value: the on-center spacing is the plant's mature spread or the planting plan; edge plants round up

soil-permeability.formula: constant head (ASTM D2434): k = Q L/(A h t); falling head (ASTM D5084): k = (a L/(A t)) ln(h1/h2); k in cm/s, 1 cm/s = 2834.6456 ft/day.
soil-permeability.edition: Darcy's-law permeameter tests -- ASTM D2434 (constant head) and ASTM D5084 (falling head) -- by name, with the Terzaghi/Das drainage-class ranges; no ASTM table text reproduced.
soil-permeability.freeAccess: Darcy's law and the two permeameter reductions are public soil-mechanics results printed in every geotechnical text; ASTM D2434/D5084 are purchased standards cited by name only.
soil-permeability.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
soil-permeability.editionNote: Soil hydraulic conductivity k from a laboratory permeameter test, the value soil-phase-relations names as out of scope. Both tests are Darcy's law v = k i solved for k. The constant-head test (ASTM D2434), for coarse free-draining soils, holds the head h fixed and collects a volume Q through a sample of length L and area A over a time t: k = Q L/(A h t). The falling-head test (ASTM D5084), for finer soils where the flow is too slow to collect a volume, times the water dropping from head h1 to h2 in a standpipe of area a: k = (a L/(A t)) ln(h1/h2). k is reported in cm/s and ft/day (1 cm/s = 2834.6 ft/day) with the standard Terzaghi/Das drainage class: above 1e-1 cm/s clean gravel, 1e-3 to 1e-1 sand, 1e-5 to 1e-3 fine or silty sand, 1e-7 to 1e-5 silt, below 1e-7 practically impervious clay. Report k at the test temperature and correct to 20 C for a standard value; a single lab specimen can miss field fabric, layering, and fractures, so field values often run higher. An engineering aid; the soil test data and the geotechnical engineer govern.

assumptions.name: Constant-head reduction
assumptions.value: k = Q L/(A h t); Darcy's law at a fixed head, for coarse soils

assumptions.name: Falling-head reduction
assumptions.value: k = (a L/(A t)) ln(h1/h2); the head falls in a standpipe of area a, for fine soils

assumptions.name: Drainage class and scope
assumptions.value: Terzaghi/Das ranges; correct to 20 C; one specimen can miss field fabric, so field k often runs higher

ballnose-feed-cusp.formula: cusp h = R - sqrt(R^2 - (w/2)^2) evaluated twice: with w = stepover for the cusp across the passes (delegated to ballnose-scallop-height) and with w = feed per tooth for the cusp along the feed. Governing cusp = max of the two; the two are equal when feed per tooth = stepover. Near the bottom both reduce to w^2/(8R). Feedrate = feed per tooth x flutes x rpm.
ballnose-feed-cusp.edition: Ballnose cusp geometry as used in CAM and mold machining. Both directions are the same circular-segment construction; nothing here is tabulated or proprietary.
ballnose-feed-cusp.freeAccess: Circular-segment geometry. No chart, table, or manufacturer data is used.
ballnose-feed-cusp.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ballnose-feed-cusp.editionNote: The reason to compute both cusps together is that only the larger one shows up on the part. A machinist who halves the stepover while leaving a coarse feed has spent cycle time on the cusp that was not governing, and the reverse mistake is just as common. The worked example is lopsided on purpose: a 1/2 in ballnose at 0.030 in stepover and 0.006 in per tooth leaves 0.000450 in across the passes against 0.000018 in along the feed, a factor of 25, so the finish is entirely a stepover question. The balance point is simple - the two cusps are equal exactly when the feed per tooth equals the stepover, because the geometry is identical in both directions. Both scale with the SQUARE of their spacing, so halving either cuts its cusp by four and doubling it quadruples it. One caution the tile states explicitly rather than leaving implied: geometric headroom on the feed is not permission to use it. Chip load, tool strength, deflection, and the machine's ability to hold the path at speed are what actually cap the feed and they usually bind first; all this says is that FINISH is not the reason to keep the feed low. These are theoretical geometric cusps on a flat surface cut at the tool tip. A sloped surface changes both the effective stepover and the effective cutting radius, and a ballnose at its tip is cutting at zero surface speed, which is its own finish problem. Tool deflection, runout, and servo behavior at direction changes all add to the real finish. Neither cusp converts to Ra: Ra is an averaged roughness and these are peak-to-valley geometry. A shop aid; the tool, the deflection, and the surface slope govern.

assumptions.name: Same geometry both ways
assumptions.value: h = R - sqrt(R^2 - (w/2)^2) with w = stepover or feed per tooth

assumptions.name: Governing cusp
assumptions.value: the larger of the two is what appears on the part

assumptions.name: Balance point
assumptions.value: the cusps are equal when feed per tooth = stepover

assumptions.name: Stepover cusp
assumptions.value: delegated to computeBallnoseScallopHeight, not reimplemented

assumptions.name: Feed headroom
assumptions.value: geometric only; chip load, deflection, and the machine usually bind first

assumptions.name: Not Ra
assumptions.value: peak-to-valley geometry on a flat surface at the tool tip; slope, deflection, and runout excluded

thrust-block-max-pressure.formula: A = (pi/4) OD^2; max_thrust = bearing_area x soil / Sf; max_pressure = max_thrust / (2 A sin(theta/2)). The inverse of Ab = Sf x 2 P A sin(theta/2) / soil, Sf ~1.5.
thrust-block-max-pressure.edition: The AWWA M41 thrust-block resultant-thrust and bearing-area method for a pipe bend, by name, solved for the pressure.
thrust-block-max-pressure.freeAccess: The resultant-thrust T = 2 P A sin(theta/2) and the bearing-area check are the standard published AWWA thrust-restraint relations.
thrust-block-max-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
thrust-block-max-pressure.editionNote: The highest pressure a thrust block of a given bearing-face area restrains at a bend, the inverse of the AWWA M41 (Ductile-Iron Pipe and Fittings) thrust-block method. The soil takes at most Ab x allowable bearing / Sf of thrust (safety factor Sf about 1.5, DIPRA; EBAA Connections PD-1), so the pressure ceiling at the bend is P = Ab x soil / (Sf x 2 A sin(theta/2)); until 2026-09-26 there was no Sf, overstating the safe pressure 1.5 times, where A is the pipe cross-sectional area from the outside diameter. The sin(theta/2) term is why a 90-degree bend restrains a lower pressure than a 45 for the same block. Compare against the test or surge pressure (not the working pressure) and use a conservative geotechnical soil-bearing value. This checks the bearing face only; the block geometry, burial depth, and the restrained-joint or passive-restraint alternative are the engineer's design. A design aid, not a substitute for the engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Max thrust from soil
assumptions.value: max thrust = bearing area x allowable soil bearing / Sf, Sf ~1.5 (input)
assumptions.source: AWWA M41 / DIPRA; EBAA Connections PD-1

assumptions.name: Pressure ceiling
assumptions.value: P = max_thrust / (2 A sin(theta/2)), A = (pi/4) OD^2

assumptions.name: Design pressure
assumptions.value: compare against the test/surge pressure and use a geotechnical soil value

siding-course-layout.formula: courses = ceil(height/target exposure); adjusted exposure = height/courses (the story-pole mark); exposure ceiling = board height - manufacturer minimum overlap; starter = wall length; course LF = courses x length.
siding-course-layout.edition: Siding story-pole layout arithmetic - no standard claimed; the exposure ceiling is the manufacturer's stated minimum headlap, entered by the user (1-in default).
siding-course-layout.freeAccess: Layout arithmetic; every siding manufacturer's installation instructions publish the exposure and overlap limits free.
siding-course-layout.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
siding-course-layout.editionNote: The judgment the tile encodes: divide the wall into WHOLE courses and shrink the exposure evenly so the top course lands full instead of a sliver. The adjustment is always safe against the overlap minimum because shrinking exposure only ever increases the lap - the ceiling check happens once, on the target. Mark the story pole at the adjusted spacing and transfer to the corners; aligning courses to window heads and sills is named as crew judgment, not automated. Squares and material are the separate siding-takeoff tile. The manufacturer's exposure limits and installation instructions govern.

assumptions.name: Whole-course adjustment
assumptions.value: courses x adjusted exposure equals the wall height exactly; the top course is always full

assumptions.name: Overlap safety
assumptions.value: shrinking exposure increases headlap, so an adjusted layout never violates a minimum the target cleared

wood-beam-shear.formula: Vr = (2/3) Fv' b d; ratio = dn/d; Vr' = (2/3) Fv' b dn (dn/d)^2; fv = 3V / (2 b dn); dcr = V / Vr'.
wood-beam-shear.edition: NDS 3.4.2 rectangular-section shear stress and the NDS 3.4.3.2 tension-side end-notch reduction, by name; the adjusted shear value comes from the NDS Supplement.
wood-beam-shear.freeAccess: The fv = 3V/(2bd) stress and the notched-member rule are stated in NDS 3.4, published free read-only by AWC at awc.org; the arithmetic is public.
wood-beam-shear.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wood-beam-shear.editionNote: The rectangular-section shear stress fv = 3V / (2 b d) (NDS 3.4.2) and the notched-bending-member rule V' = (2/3) Fv' b dn (dn/d)^2 for a notch on the tension side at the end of a bending member (NDS 3.4.3.2). Fv' is the reference shear value already multiplied by every applicable adjustment factor - the user supplies it, and the reference Fv and the factors come from the NDS Supplement for the actual species, grade, and service condition. This is the tension-side end-notch case only, and does not cover notches on the compression side (a different rule), notches away from the support, the special provisions for sloped or bevel-cut notches, round notches, or the Cvr shear-reduction factor for members with connections in the shear zone; loads within a distance d of the support may be neglected in V per NDS 3.4.3.1, which the user applies to the input. A design aid, not a substitute for the engineer of record.

assumptions.name: Notch penalty
assumptions.value: the (dn/d)^2 factor squares the depth ratio, so a tension-side notch cuts the allowable end shear far faster than the depth loss alone

assumptions.name: Fv' user-supplied
assumptions.value: Fv' is the reference shear value times every applicable factor; the reference and factors come from the NDS Supplement

assumptions.name: Loads near support
assumptions.value: loads within a distance d of the support may be neglected in V per NDS 3.4.3.1; the user applies that to the input

manual-d-friction-rate.formula: ASP = blower_ESP - component_drops; FR = ASP x 100 / TEL (in wg per 100 ft).
manual-d-friction-rate.edition: The ACCA Manual D friction rate (available static pressure over total effective length), by name.
manual-d-friction-rate.freeAccess: The available-static-pressure and friction-rate relations are the published ACCA Manual D residential duct-design method.
manual-d-friction-rate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
manual-d-friction-rate.editionNote: The ACCA Manual D friction rate: the available static pressure ASP = the blower's rated external static at design CFM minus the sum of the component pressure drops (coil, filter, registers/grilles, dampers, balancing), and the design friction rate FR = ASP x 100 / the total effective length (in wg per 100 ft). The TEL is the longest supply-plus-return path including the equivalent lengths of the fittings, not the physical run. A typical FR target is 0.06-0.10; a lower rate requires larger ducts. This returns the ASP and FR; it does not size the individual ducts (that is the Manual D duct chart / ductulator step). A design aid; the full Manual D layout governs.

assumptions.name: Available static
assumptions.value: ASP = blower ESP - total component drops

assumptions.name: Friction rate
assumptions.value: FR = ASP x 100 / total effective length

assumptions.name: TEL
assumptions.value: longest supply+return path incl. fitting equivalent lengths

weibull-capacity-factor.formula: the Weibull pdf f(v) = (k/c)(v/c) raised to (k-1) times exp of minus (v/c) raised to k; mean speed = c x Gamma(1 + 1/k); energy pattern factor = Gamma(1 + 3/k) / Gamma(1 + 1/k) cubed; annual energy is that distribution integrated against a curve cubic from cut-in to rated and flat to cut-out; capacity factor = annual energy / (rated power x 8,760 hours).
weibull-capacity-factor.edition: The two-parameter Weibull distribution, the energy pattern factor, and the capacity-factor definition by name, with IEC 61400-12 named for the measurement campaign that fits the parameters. An independent energy assessor and the manufacturer's warranted power curve govern a bankable estimate.
weibull-capacity-factor.freeAccess: An integral over the user's own Weibull parameters and machine ratings; no wind atlas, measured dataset, or manufacturer power curve is reproduced.
weibull-capacity-factor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
weibull-capacity-factor.editionNote: The energy pattern factor is the number that makes the point: at a shape parameter of 2 the mean of the cubes is about 1.9 times the cube of the mean, so an energy estimate built on average wind speed alone is low by nearly half. Every serious wind calculation is an integral of the power curve against the distribution for exactly that reason, and the shape parameter controls how pronounced the effect is. Capacity factor then puts the result in a comparable form -- it is the honest measure of a site and a machine together and it is what makes a large rotor on a modest tower comparable with a small rotor on a tall one; a figure claimed above about 60% onshore deserves the same scepticism as a power coefficient above Betz. The hours matter as much as the energy: a site can look windy on its mean and still spend a large share of the year below cut-in making nothing at all, and a mean speed hides that completely. Fitting the parameters requires a year or more of measured data at or near hub height, and parameters from a wind atlas or a nearby station are indicative only.

assumptions.name: The distribution, not the mean
assumptions.value: an average-speed estimate is low by roughly the energy pattern factor

assumptions.name: The curve here is an idealisation
assumptions.value: cubic to rated then flat; a real machine's curve is not that

assumptions.name: Losses are 10 to 20% combined
assumptions.value: wake, availability, electrical, soiling, icing, curtailment

valve-actuator-close-off.formula: seat force = differential pressure x effective seat area, evaluated at the differential at MINIMUM system flow rather than at design; the actuator's rated close-off is converted to a force the same way and compared; the spring-direction rating is compared separately.
valve-actuator-close-off.edition: Valve close-off as control-valve practice states it. The effective seat area and both actuator ratings are ENTERED from the manufacturer's tables; on a rotary valve close-off is published as a TORQUE and this force basis does not apply. It does not size the valve or its Cv, compute the minimum-flow differential (which needs the pump curve and the system), evaluate valve authority (valve-authority does), or address cavitation and flashing.
valve-actuator-close-off.freeAccess: One product and one comparison; no manufacturer table is reproduced.
valve-actuator-close-off.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
valve-actuator-close-off.editionNote: The differential a valve must close against is not the one it sees at design flow. As other valves close, the pump rides up its curve and the pressure across the remaining valves rises toward shutoff head, so the worst case is MINIMUM system flow -- the condition a designer computing at design never looks at, and the condition in which the valve is most likely to be commanded shut. The consequence of getting it wrong is subtle: the valve strokes, the actuator reports closed, and a small flow continues past the seat, so a zone overheats and the problem reads as a control fault. Spring-return actuators get their own line because their spring-direction close-off is often much lower, which means a valve that holds on command can leak on a power failure.

assumptions.name: The effective seat area is entered
assumptions.value: it is not the nominal valve size

assumptions.name: Rotary valves use torque
assumptions.value: the force basis here does not apply to ball or butterfly valves

assumptions.name: The minimum-flow differential is entered
assumptions.value: it needs the pump curve and the system to compute

walkway-clearing-productivity.formula: machine time = open walk area / (blower rate x depth factor); hand time = hand area / (shovellers x hand rate x depth factor); the crew time is the LARGER of the two, not the sum; crews = crew time / service window, rounded up; ice melt = area / 1,000 x the rate, PER APPLICATION.
walkway-clearing-productivity.edition: The parallel-operation crew time convention. Production rates and depth factors are ENTERED from the contractor's own timed records.
walkway-clearing-productivity.freeAccess: Two rate divisions and a maximum.
walkway-clearing-productivity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
walkway-clearing-productivity.editionNote: THE SPEC THIS IMPLEMENTS STATES A CONCLUSION ITS OWN NUMBERS REFUTE. spec-v1850 says the 12 in case 'fails on the hand work, which is what degrades fastest', but its own depth factors -- the blower at a quarter of its rate, hand work at a third -- give 3.33 h of machine work against 2.50 h of hand work. THE MACHINE GOVERNS, and it degraded faster, not slower. Which operation governs is therefore COMPUTED from the entered rates and factors and named in the output, and a crew whose two operations finish together is reported as balanced rather than having one arbitrarily declared the leader. That matters operationally, because the whole point of the parallel model is that adding capacity to the operation which is NOT governing changes nothing at all. The material is counted PER APPLICATION, not per storm: a walk cleared once and then left to refreeze is worse than one never cleared, and the re-application is the part most often left out of both the material order and the labour estimate. The two operations are treated as perfectly parallel and independent, which they are not.

assumptions.name: Perfectly parallel operations
assumptions.value: crews interfere, share transport, and lose time between properties

assumptions.name: Rates and depth factors are entered
assumptions.value: illustrative rather than measured; they do not transfer between properties

assumptions.name: Travel between sites is not counted
assumptions.value: on a route of small sites it commonly exceeds the clearing time

radio-site-duty-cycle-battery.formula: average current = transmit duty x transmit A + receive duty x receive A + standby duty x standby A (default 5/5/90); Ah for runtime = average A x hours; nameplate Ah = runtime Ah / usable depth of discharge; daily Ah = average A x 24 h.
radio-site-duty-cycle-battery.edition: The 5-5-90 duty cycle convention (5% transmit, 5% receive, 90% standby) as published in radio manufacturers' battery-life specifications, for example the Motorola Solutions BPR40 data sheet, named as the default; the equipment manufacturer's current draws and the site's measured traffic named as governing.
radio-site-duty-cycle-battery.freeAccess: A weighted average on currents and duties the user enters; no manufacturer table is reproduced.
radio-site-duty-cycle-battery.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
radio-site-duty-cycle-battery.editionNote: Transmit current is many times receive current, but a radio spends most of its time listening, so the duty-weighted average sits far nearer the standby draw than the transmit draw. The 5-5-90 split is the convention manufacturers use to state battery life and is a reasonable default for a base station or a portable in routine use. A repeater is the case where it is wrong: it retransmits every user on the channel, so during an incident its transmit fraction can be several times 5%, and the site's measured or expected duty must be entered instead. Daily ampere-hours are reported because a site that must run indefinitely is sized by its recharge -- the solar array or generator run hours must replace a day's use every day. Temperature, aging, Peukert effects, and converter losses are outside the estimate.

assumptions.name: 5-5-90 default duty
assumptions.value: 5% transmit, 5% receive, 90% standby
assumptions.source: radio manufacturer battery-life specifications (e.g., Motorola Solutions BPR40)

assumptions.name: Repeater duty
assumptions.value: a repeater transmits whenever any user talks; enter measured or expected site duty

assumptions.name: Usable depth of discharge
assumptions.value: nameplate Ah = required Ah / usable fraction
